analysis.one_liner: Lets Labor seize garments from repeat sweatshop violators and sharply raises penalties for wage law violations.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Rep. Chuck Schumer with no cosponsors, referred to committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cracked down on garment-industry sweatshops. It raised the money employers must pay workers they cheat on minimum wage and overtime, increased civil and criminal fines, and let the Secretary of Labor seize garments from manufacturers who repeatedly violate wage laws or use illegal home-based labor. It also stretched the time limit for workers to sue over unpaid wages from two years to three, and required federal and state enforcers to share information about violators.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage garment workers, many of them immigrants, who are denied minimum wage, overtime, or legal working conditions. Workers would recover more of what they were owed (triple damages for repeat violations plus interest), have three years instead of two to sue, and benefit from tighter coordination between wage, safety, and immigration enforcers. Honest manufacturers who comply with the law would also face less underpriced competition from violators.

how_it_helps.text: Repeat violators of minimum wage and overtime rules would owe workers three times their unpaid wages, and even first-time violators would owe liquidated damages plus interest [S3].

The Secretary of Labor could seize garments from the premises of a garment manufacturer who violates wage or child labor standards more than twice in three years, up to the employer's liability; garments made by unauthorized homeworkers could be seized entirely [S3].

Civil penalties for repeat wage and child labor violations would rise to as much as $10,000 per violation, and criminal violators would face at least six months and up to one year of imprisonment instead of a maximum of six months [S3].
The window for workers to sue over unpaid minimum wages, overtime, or related damages would extend from two years to three years [S3].

Labor Department and OSHA enforcers would be required to share information about suspected violators with each other, the Immigration and Naturalization Service, and state labor departments, with cross-training of staff [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Garment manufacturers and contractors who violate wage, hour, or homework laws would pay higher damages, fines, and could lose their goods to seizure. Compliant businesses would face the same enforcement regime but no new substantive obligations beyond the longer statute of limitations.

drawbacks.text: Critics of aggressive garment seizures have long argued they can penalize manufacturers and brand owners who may not directly control contractors' labor practices, since the bill allows seizure of garments on a violator's premises even though separate contractors often did the sewing [S3].

Higher penalties and a longer window for lawsuits raise litigation and compliance costs for the garment industry generally, not only for willful violators, which honest supporters would acknowledge as a real cost [S3].

The bill's information-sharing between labor enforcers and immigration authorities raises the concern that immigrant workers could fear contacting enforcement agencies, potentially chilling complaints from the very workers the bill aims to protect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefits are concrete: more complete recovery of stolen wages, more time to sue, and a credible threat against repeat violators. The costs fall mainly on violators, though seizures and higher penalties could sweep in some businesses at the margin of contractor networks. On balance the design is a straightforward enforcement-strengthening bill with the usual tradeoff of tougher penalties against possible overreach in seizure cases.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Labor Standards Subcommittee, where it sat; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chuck Schumer introduced the bill on January 3, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S5].
On February 8, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, and the record shows no further action for the rest of the 102nd Congress [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sweatshop operators and garment manufacturers who underpay workers, since no stronger penalties or seizure power was ever enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who violate wage and hour laws

for.name: Rep. Charles E. Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Sweatshops Prevention Act and referred it to committee; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: Subcommittee on Labor Standards
against.role: House Education and Labor subcommittee holding the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 8, 1991 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for votes, so no roll-call record exists; it had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.note: Repeat violators would owe triple unpaid wages, face fines up to $10,000 per violation, and risk having their garments seized. Compliant firms would gain from less underpriced competition, but the bill's costs fall squarely on violators and the businesses around them.

Garments produced by homeworkers in violation of the FLSA's homework rules could be seized in full, even when a homeworker certificate had been issued. This targets a sector where underpaid home labor is hard to inspect.
